Learning Objectives
Describe relevant humeral anatomy.
Recognize humeral shaft fracture patterns and mechanisms of injury.
Perform a proper physical examination and imaging workup for a patient with a humeral shaft
fracture.
Identify indications for surgical and nonsurgical management of humeral shaft fractures.
Describe surgical approaches for the management of humeral shaft fractures.
Discuss complications of the management of humeral shaft fractures.

Humeral shaft fractures account for 1% to 3% of all fractures.
20% of humeral fractures involve the shaft.
Most commonly occur in the middle third of the bone.
Bimodal age distribution: males in their twenties and females in their sixties
Young age group: high-energy trauma more frequently the cause
Lower energy mechanisms of injury are more common in older patients.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The anatomy of the humerus varies throughout its length (Figure 1).
The shaft generally is cylindrical.
Distally, the humerus becomes triangular.
The intramedullary canal tapers and terminates approximately 2 to 3 cm proximal to the
olecranon fossa.
Medial and lateral intermuscular septa delineate the posterior and anterior compartments of
the arm.

Vascular Anatomy
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery Anatomy (Figure 2).
The brachial artery contributes to the deep brachial artery (profunda artery).
The profunda artery travels with the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

The main neurologic structures of the arm and forearm traverse the soft tissues overlying the
humerus (Figures 2 and 3).
Posteriorly, the spiral groove houses the radial nerve.
The spiral groove is directly posterior to the deltoid tuberosity.

The radial nerve can be found approximately 14 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle
and 20 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, traversing the posterior aspect of the
humerus. Radial nerve palsy is observed in 11.8% of patients with a humeral shaft
fracture. A Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal one-third of the

Injury Classification
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification system uses a combination
of numbers and letters to describe the fracture: bone number (humerus = 1); location
(diaphysis = 2); fracture pattern (simple = A, wedge = B, complex = C); and severity (1 through
3) (Figure 4).
The descriptive classification system is based on the location relative to the pectoralis and the
deltoid. It provides information about the relative direction and displacement of the main
fracture fragments.
A classification system based on fracture characteristics (transverse, oblique, spiral, segmental,
comminuted) may aid in determining management.

Fracture pattern is related to the mechanism of injury and bone quality.
Careful patient history is important to rule out pathologic processes that would require
additional workup.
The mechanism of injury should match the fracture pattern.

Patient History
The humerus is the second most commonly involved long bone with pathologic fractures
(complete or impending fractures). Common malignancies that metastasize to bone are
breast, prostate, kidney, thyroid, and lung malignancies. Multiple myeloma also can
cause pathologic fractures of the humeral shaft (Figure 5).
Spiral fractures of the humerus indicate a rotational force. A mechanism of injury that
does not match the fracture pattern is a potential sign of domestic or child abuse.

breast cancer metastasis. A pathologic lesion is observed in the humeral shaft, which
resulted in the fracture. (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD, Phoenix, AZ.)
Physical Examination
Inspect skin for open wounds.
Palpate joints/bones above and below fracture
Assess for radial pulse
Motor examination of upper extremity
Sensory examination of hand and forearm

Physical Examination
The surgeon must document a detailed neurologic examination before and after any
intervention for the fracture: splinting, reduction, or surgical management. If neurologic
function cannot be assessed secondary to pain or the patient is unable to cooperate with
the examination, then documentation that the neurologic examination could not be
obtained secondary to the patient being unable to cooperate or participate is essential.
Extension of the interphalangeal joints of the fingers is not a radial nerve function; this
may be misleading if the arm/wrist is in a splint.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP and lateral views of the humerus (Figure 6).
If obtaining a transthoracic lateral view, rotating the patient prevents rotation of the distal
fragment and avoids the risk of additional soft-tissue or nerve injury.
The radiographic series should include the shoulder and elbow (joint above and joint below) to
rule out associated injuries (Figure 6).
SEND FEEDBACK

Good quality imaging studies are essential in determining how to properly manage humeral
shaft fractures. Failure to obtain quality images may adversely affect treatment decisions
(Figure 7).
Figure 6 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the humeral shaft demonstrate visualization of the
shoulder and elbow joints (joints above and below). (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD, Phoenix,
AZ.)

Figure 7 Radiographs of the arm of a polytrauma patient with multiple upper extremity fractures.
Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the humeral shaft demonstrate a segmental
humeral shaft fracture. The elbow joint is not well visualized on the lateral view. C, Preoperative
lateral radiograph of the elbow demonstrates associated olecranon and ulnar shaft fractures.
Postoperative lateral (D) and AP (E) radiographs demonstrate surgical fixation of the humerus.
Mini-fragment plates were used as reduction aids because of the unstable segmental fracture,
and a large fragment plate with 4.5-mm screws was used for definitive fixation. Surgical fixation
of the olecranon and the ulnar shaft also was performed. (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD,
Phoenix, AZ.)
CT and MRI
Pathologic process suspected/metastatic disease
Assess for potential intra-articular extension proximally or distally
CT may be useful in detecting intra-articular extension of a proximal or distal humeral shaft
fracture. CT also may help to determine if a fracture may be pathologic (Figure 8)
MRI can detect stress fractures of the humeral shaft. Stress fractures of the humeral shaft may
be observed in throwing/overhead athletes and weightlifters (Resource 3)

Indications
Fracture with acceptable alignment
No consensus exists on acceptable alignment; however, the following have been proposed as
acceptable: 20° of apex anterior or posterior angulation, 30° of varus/valgus angulation, 15°
of malrotation, and 3 cm of shortening (Figure 8).
Nonsurgical candidate secondary to comorbidities
Closed fracture
Low-velocity gunshot injury (Figure 8)

Indications
Similar to every orthopaedic patient, treatment options, risks, and advantages of surgical
and nonsurgical treatment should be discussed with the patient and documented in the
medical record.
Contraindications
Open fracture
Polytrauma
Floating elbow (Figure 7)
Inability to maintain reduction with fracture brace because of body habitus (Figure 9)
Inability to maintain reduction or a fracture with unacceptable alignment (Figure 10)
Failed nonsurgical management (Figure 11)
Brachial plexus injury
Vascular injury necessitating repair

shoulder (A), lateral (B) and oblique (C) elbow, and lateral shoulder (D) radiographs demonstrate
a displaced fracture of the upper third of the humeral shaft. E, Coronal CT scan of the torso
shows a large body habitus and morbid obesity. F, Clinical photograph of the arm shows the large
size of the soft tissues, which will make nonsurgical management difficult because of inability to
attain or maintain reduction with the use of a brace. AP (G) and lateral (H) fluoroscopic images
show intramedullary fixation of the fracture with the use of an intramedullary nail. Note the
medial insertion point of the nail. AP (I) and lateral (J) fluoroscopic images show statically locked
fixation proximally and distally. (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD, Phoenix, AZ.)

Management
Preferred treatment option for most humeral shaft fractures. Historical literature has reported
good results with these techniques.
Closed management may involve initial coaptation splinting followed by a functional brace or a
hanging arm cast (Figure 12).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Humeral Shaft
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001188
17/38

More recent studies suggest the failure rate of nonsurgical management may be as high as
25% to 30%.1-5
Hanging arm casts may be considered for shortened oblique, spiral, and transverse fractures.
Figure 12 Images of a patient with a humerus fracture. A, AP radiograph of the humerus
demonstrates a midshaft fracture. B, AP radiograph of the humerus obtained at 3-month follow-
up demonstrates healing and corrected angulation after management with the use of a
Sarmiento brace. C, Photograph shows the patient wearing a Sarmiento brace. (Reproduced from
Carroll EA, Schweppe M, Langfitt M, Miller AN, Halvorson JJ: Management of humeral shaft
fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[7]:423-433.)

Management
The coaptation splint is used for 7 to 10 days, after which a fracture brace is applied in
the office. Weekly radiographs to assess alignment have been questioned. Immediately
on fracture brace application, the patient is encouraged to perform pendulum exercises
for shoulder mobility. Isometric biceps, triceps, and deltoid muscle exercises and active
wrist and hand exercises also are encouraged. The patient is instructed to adjust the
tension of the fracture brace as necessary and to sleep in a semi-erect position until 4 to
6 weeks postinjury. The fracture brace is worn for 10 to 12 weeks, until no pain or
mobility is present with palpation at the fracture site, more than 90° of shoulder and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Humeral Shaft
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001188
18/38

elbow motion is painless, and bridging callus is observed radiographically on three of
four cortices. If motion is detected at the fracture site on physical examination and
minimal callus is observed on radiographs at 6 weeks postinjury, a near-100% likelihood
of nonunion exists, and surgical treatment should be discussed with the patient.
Hanging arm casts may be considered for shortened oblique, spiral, and transverse
fractures. The cast should extend from 2 cm proximal to the fracture, across the 90°
flexed elbow, and to the wrist; the forearm should be in neutral rotation. Suspension
straps are attached to loops on the forearm aspect of the cast to aid in alignment.
A recently published randomized controlled trial comparing surgical fixation with
nonsurgical management reported a 25% risk of nonunion with nonsurgical
management.5
Surgical Management
Relative Indications
Open fracture (Table 1)
Brachial plexus injury
Failed nonsurgical management
Bracing not possible because of body habitus (Figure 9)
Bracing not tolerated
Inadequate alignment (Figure 10)
Lack of union with nonsurgical management (Figure 11)
Impending or complete pathologic fracture (Figures 5 and 13)
Polytrauma
Floating elbow (ipsilateral with forearm or elbow fracture [Figure 7])
Morbid obesity (Figure 9)
Lower extremity fractures; necessary upper extremity weight bearing


Patient Positioning
Patient positioning for the procedure is determined by the surgical exposure and
surgeon preference. The key for a successful surgical procedure is having a well-thought-
out plan, proper equipment, and adequate approach/exposure of the fracture.
Awareness of the radial nerve in relation to the fracture location and the surgical
approach is essential to avoid complications. If the radial nerve is close to the surgical
field, it should be identified to ensure it is not injured during the procedure or trapped
under the plate. If the anterior approach is used, the radial nerve can be located distally
between the brachialis and brachioradialis and traced up as it traverses from the
anterior compartment to the posterior compartment (Figure 2). If the posterior
approach is used, the radial nerve should be identified at the mid-aspect of the humeral
shaft, the location at which it pierces the posterior compartment (Figures 3 and 14).

Figure 14 Illustration of a shoulder shows the posterior triceps-splitting approach, which
provides access to the distal 76% of the humeral diaphysis after the radial nerve is
mobilized. With this approach, the long and lateral heads of the triceps are separated,
after which intramuscular division of the medial head of the triceps is performed.
Proximal extension is limited by the lateral head of the triceps. (Adapted with permission
from Gerwin M, Hotchkiss RN, Weiland AJ: Alternative operative exposures of the
posterior aspect of the humeral diaphysis: With reference to the radial nerve. J Bone Joint
Surg Am 1996;78[11]:1690-1695.)
Open Reduction and Plate Fixation
Fixation with the use of plate-and-screw constructs is associated with union rates as high as
94%, with low infection rates (zero to 6%) and a low incidence of iatrogenic nerve injury (zero
to 5%); it also allows patients with multiple injuries to bear weight through the injured
extremity (Figure 15).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Humeral Shaft
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001188
23/38

Conventional plating usually is performed with the use of a broad, 4.5-mm plate and three or
four screws per side for axial and torsional stability.
To improve resistance to bending with the use of a long plate, screw placement should include
near-near and far-far relative to the site of the fracture.
In osteoporotic bone, locked plating has been shown to improve stability and resistance to
torsional stresses.
The technique of minimally invasive plating osteosynthesis has been described; however,
clinical advantages over traditional open reduction and internal fixation have not yet been
demonstrated.
Figure 15 Radiographs of a humeral shaft with a fracture managed via open reduction and
internal fixation. Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate a fracture of the
mid-shaft of the humerus. Given the transverse nature of the fracture, which is associated with
an increased risk of nonunion; poor alignment; and patient preference, surgical management
was performed. Postoperative AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs demonstrate anatomic
alignment and fixation with the use of a plate and screws. (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD,
Phoenix, AZ.)
Intramedullary Nailing
Advocated by some as an alternative to plate fixation (Video 2).
Originally, nonlocking flexible nails were used and inserted in an antegrade or retrograde
fashion; however, newer interlocking nails have become more common, allow for better
rotational control, and should be considered the standard of care during humeral nailing
(Figures 9 and 13).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Humeral Shaft
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001188
24/38

Intramedullary nails may be useful in segmental fractures, in the multiply injured patient to
limit positioning changes, and in pathologic fractures (Figure 13).
Intramedullary nails have been shown to withstand higher axial and bending loads than plates;
however, plated humerus fractures have been clinically shown to allow for full–weight bearing
and have not been associated with a higher incidence of malunion or nonunion.
Intramedullary nailing of humerus fractures has been shown to result in a higher incidence of
shoulder pain from injury to the rotator cuff and a potential risk to neurovascular structures
with reaming or with the use of locking long nails distally.
The humeral canal tapers to an end distally above the olecranon fossa, and selection of nail
length is critical. Attempting to seat a nail that is too long proximally to avoid cuff irritation may
lead to distraction at the fracture site; this substantially increases the rate of delayed union
and nonunion.

Patient positioning for the procedure is determined by the surgical exposure and
surgeon preference. The key for a successful surgical procedure is having a well-thought-
out plan, proper equipment, and adequate approach/exposure of the fracture.
With the use of locked intramedullary nails, a greater mismatch of nail diameter and
shape occur with retrograde nailing than antegrade nailing and substantially more
reaming is necessary, which may increase bone weakness and the risk of a
supracondylar fracture. The radial nerve is at risk with the use of a lateral-to-medial
distal locking screw. The musculocutaneous nerve is at risk with the use of an anterior-
to-posterior locking screw (Figures 2 and 3).
Comparison of plating with nailing for the management of humeral shaft fractures has
shown that plating results in less need for revision surgery, a lower nonunion rate, and
fewer shoulder problems (Resources 4 and 5).
External Fixation
Staged external fixation is indicated for severe soft-tissue injury, bone defects, vascular injury
with acute repair, medically unstable patients, and infected nonunions (Figure 16).
During external fixation, care must be taken to avoid neurovascular structures (Figures 2 and
3).

Figure 16 Images of the humeral shaft of a polytrauma patient who sustained multiple gunshot
injuries. A, AP radiograph demonstrates a complex segmental fracture. Given the critical status of
the patient, external fixation was applied to stabilize the fracture until the patient was
resuscitated and optimized for definitive surgical fixation. AP radiograph (B) and lateral (C) and AP

ulna. Note that the fracture is pulled out to length. (Courtesy of Niloofar Dehghan, MD, Phoenix,
AZ.)

External Fixation
Typically, the elbow joint is spanned with the use of two lateral pins placed proximal to
the fracture in the humeral diaphysis and two pins in the ulna or radius, depending on
whether a forearm injury is present. The ulna is the preferred location for pin placement,
if possible, because of its subcutaneous location, the limited risk to neurovascular
structures, and the ability to maintain pronation-supination mobility during the period of
external fixation. An open approach is recommended for the humeral pins because of
the variability of nerve courses in the region. An open approach also should be used if
the distal pins are placed in the radius (Figure 16).
Surgical Approaches
Dictated by anatomic location of fracture (Table 2).
Anterolateral approach: an extensile approach; usually considered for proximal third to middle
third humeral shaft fractures.

9/3/26, 4:14 PM

Posterior approach: ideal for distal third fractures and most effective for the distal two-thirds
of the shaft from the deltoid insertion and distally; the deltoid muscle prevents extension of
this approach proximally to the shoulder (Figure 14).
Other approaches (Resource 6)
Percutaneous, anterior, anteromedial, and direct lateral approaches have been described and
may be used based on wound considerations, other injuries (eg, need for associated vascular
repair), or the need for other approaches based on concomitant injuries.

Surgical Approaches
The radial nerve can be identified distally between the brachialis and brachioradialis
muscles and traced proximally as it pierces the intermuscular septum. The brachialis
(innervated by the radial and musculocutaneous nerves) is split to spare its dual
innervation and protect the radial nerve during retraction. The anterolateral approach
can be extended proximally into the deltopectoral approach to the proximal humerus.
The posterior approach can be performed via a triceps-sparing or triceps-splitting
approach, depending on the fracture location. Identification and protection of the radial
nerve, and ulnar nerve (if working on the medial side), are imperative with this approach.
The radial nerve can be found approximately 14 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle
and 20 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, traversing the posterior aspect of the
humerus. The radial nerve also can be identified by finding the lower lateral brachial
cutaneous nerve laterally and tracing it proximally to the radial nerve adjacent to the
spiral groove.
The ulnar nerve emerges medially from deep to the medial head of the triceps. It
courses distally through the cubital tunnel. It can be palpated along the medial aspect of
the triceps along the distal third of the humerus. If the medial aspect of the distal
humeral shaft is exposed, such as during the paratricipital approach, location and
protection of the ulnar nerve are imperative.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
To minimize shoulder pain, a medial starting point for antegrade intramedullary nailing has
been suggested (Figures 9, G and 13, C). Although articular cartilage at the zenith of the head
is violated, the rotator cuff in this area is well vascularized for healing and away from the usual
impingement zone.
If plating via a posterior approach, the radial nerve must be identified and protected (Figure
14).

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
The interval between the anterior and middle thirds of the deltoid is split, and an inline-
splitting incision of the rotator cuff is made. This allows for a direct path to the
intramedullary canal and easier side-to-side tendon closure.
The surgeon must be aware that the humeral canal ends 2 to 3 cm proximal to the
olecranon fossa and narrows distally, which may result in a risk for fracture distraction if
impacting the nail.
Complications
Nonunion
Although union rates are relatively high with humeral shaft fractures, nonunions can occur.
Motion, avascularity, smoking, metabolic deficiency, and infection are potential causes of
nonunion.
Fractures adjacent to a stiff joint have a higher risk of nonunion because of increased motion
at the fracture site (such as proximal humeral shaft fractures patients with preexisting
shoulder arthritis).
Technical error in fixation, fracture distraction, and inadequate plate size also may lead to
nonunion (Figure 17).
Fractures at higher risk of nonunion are those with distraction and transverse fracture
pattern (compared with comminuted fractures).
In patients with osteopenia and osteoporosis, stability can be achieved with the use of locked
plates.
Infected nonunion
Eradication of the infection is important to achieve union.
In select patients with severe infection, temporary or definitive external fixation in
combination with resection of affected tissue and antibiotic treatment may be required.
Whether required by atrophic nonunion or infection, resection and shortening of as much as
4 cm can be tolerated.

Closed humeral shaft fractures with no callus formation and gross fracture site
movement at 6 weeks postinjury are associated with an almost 100% positive predictive
value of progressing to nonunion. Surgical management is indicated in this setting
(Resource 7; Figure 11).

Malunion
The mobile nature of the shoulder joint allows a degree of axial, angular, and rotational
deformity with a malunion to be well tolerated. Therefore, knowledge of prior shoulder
injuries or loss of shoulder motion is important in deciding how to properly manage a
humeral shaft fracture (Resource 8).

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Radial nerve palsy
Humerus fractures often are associated with radial nerve palsies from the time of injury, from
attempted closed reduction, or during surgical management.
A recent meta-analysis of 4,517 fractures reported an overall 11.8% incidence of concomitant
radial nerve palsies in transverse and spiral fractures, with the middle and distal third of the
humeral shaft most frequently involved.4

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Almost all patients with radial nerve neurapraxia recover. Substantially different rates of
recovery are reported for complete (78%) versus incomplete (98%) palsies and closed
(97%) versus open (86%) injuries. Barring open injury, vascular injury, a segmental
fracture, or floating elbow, no difference has been noted in recovery after early or late
exploration. For a concomitant nerve injury in patients who do not require surgical
management of a fracture, electromyography and/or nerve conduction velocity studies
should be performed 6 weeks postinjury. In patients who require surgical treatment,
exploration is performed at the time of surgical treatment.
For secondary palsies that occur after fracture reduction, no evidence has shown that
surgical management improves the ultimate recovery rate compared with nonsurgical
management. Delayed surgical exploration should be performed after 3 to 4 months if
no evidence of recovery is apparent via electromyography or nerve conduction velocity
studies. Recently, ultrasonography has been used to evaluate the continuity of the radial
nerve (Resources 10 and 11).
Interlocking with humeral nails may place the axillary nerve at risk proximally and the
lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, median nerve, radial nerve, or brachial artery at
risk distally. These risks can be minimized via a limited open approach, with careful blunt
dissection to bone when applying interlocking screws (Figures 2, 3, and 13, F).
When passing the reamer through an area of comminution, the reamer should be
turned off and pushed through the area manually to avoid damage to the radial nerve. If
radial nerve dysfunction is present preoperatively and intramedullary nailing is selected,
a limited open approach should be considered to ensure that the fracture site is clear of
neurovascular structures before nail placement.

Vascular injury is rare and may be the result of a penetrating injury (eg, industrial accident,
gunshot wound). Revascularization should be performed within 6 hours postinjury.
Rehabilitation
Patients with a humeral shaft fracture managed nonsurgically should undergo rehabilitation.
Depending on the fracture location, range of motion of the shoulder and elbow may be
possible immediately to prevent stiffness.
Patients with a surgically managed humeral shaft fracture do not require immobilization.
Range of motion of the shoulder and elbow can begin immediately and progress as tolerated.
Patients with a fracture managed via plate fixation may be allowed bear weight as tolerated
immediately postoperatively (eg, a polytrauma patient is allowed to bear weight on upper
extremities and use crutches). Resistance strengthening exercises may begin postoperatively
or, if nonsurgical management is performed, after callus is evident and no motion or pain is
present at the fracture site. Full-crutch–weight bearing does not influence the healing of
humeral shaft fractures managed via open reduction and internal fixation (Resources 12 and
13).
Outcomes
Open fractures are associated with a 12% infection rate without fixation and a 10.8% infection
rate with fixation.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Document a careful neurologic examination preoperative and postoperatively; postoperative
nerve palsy is the surgeon’s responsibility if not clearly documented preoperatively.
Assess treatment plan for each patient individually; no cookbook approach exists.
Discuss and document the risk of radial nerve palsy associated with surgical treatment with
patients.
Recognize the fracture pattern and location.
Template the fixation plan.
Assess the planned surgical approach.
Determine the approach that will allow for the safe placement of hardware
